extracted.intended_audience: state regulators, power plant owners/operators, industry stakeholders, and environmental law/practice participants involved in CAA section 111(d) state plan development
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance explaining EPA determinations of the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and related standards for existing coal-, natural gas-, and oil-fired steam generating units under CAA section 111(d). Includes technical feasibility, cost reasonableness, compliance dates, subcategory definitions, and degrees of emission limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co-firing at 40% as BSER for medium-term coal-fired units
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing natural gas co-firing at a level of 40 percent of annual heat input as the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the finalized BSER choice for the medium-term subcategory based on the subcategory-specific analysis described throughout the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated: operational evidence for co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas co-firing at 40% is 'adequately demonstrated' because many existing coal-fired units already use natural gas and several have co-fired at or above 40% of heat input (29 units co-fired >=60% hourly and 29 units co-fired >40% annual heat input during 2015–2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats existing operational experience (units demonstrating high-hour or high-annual co-firing shares) as evidence of technical feasibility and applicability across the fleet; see the technical support document (TSD) for facility-level detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler modification feasibility and typical modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing coal-fired boilers can be modified to co-fire natural gas up to 100% by installing new gas burners and related modifications (new fuel supply lines, air duct changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes potential small impacts on boiler efficiency (due to natural gas hydrogen content); net heat rate impacts can range from a 2% increase to a 2% decrease. Project-specific scope depends on existing configuration and desired co-firing level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas pipeline lateral development as enabling requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase natural gas access, facilities without sufficient gas access may need lateral pipeline construction to connect to the transmission network; pipeline capacity must be sized for needed peak/average gas use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA estimated laterals sized to meet 60% of net summer capacity would be sufficient to enable 40% annual co-firing. Lateral cost and feasibility depend on length, diameter (capacity), number of laterals, and proximity to existing transmission pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline system upstream capacity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assessed whether existing transmission systems could satisfy peak capacity implied by new laterals without transmission system modification and found that most (if not all) existing pipeline systems could meet peak needs in aggregate under conservative assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assessment used a conservative scenario (all analyzed EGUs co-fire at levels implied by laterals, e.g., 60% net summer capacity). Individual project routing/connection feasibility still requires project-level study and permitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical lateral lengths and aggregate pipeline requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Most individual laterals are less than 15 miles. Maximum aggregate capacity for implementing 40% co-firing across the eligible fleet estimated at ~14.7 billion cubic feet per day, ~3,500 miles of pipeline, costing roughly $11.5 billion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA translates aggregate build into annualized figures (e.g., <1,800 miles and ~$5.75 billion per year over 2 years in the conservative scenario) and compares to historical and industry-projected pipeline construction to show comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline cost metric (dollars per inch-mile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lateral development cost averaged approximately $280,000 per inch-mile (2019$) in the contiguous U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total lateral cost is calculated from this per-inch-mile metric combined with required pipeline diameter (capacity) and length; site-specific factors can cause variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date for medium-term coal-fired units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a compliance date of January 1, 2030 for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeline assumptions: feasibility work during state plan development (12 months for pipeline lateral, 6 months for boiler modifications between June 2024–June 2025); permitting and construction timelines based on recent pipeline projects (permitting+approval <1.5 years avg; construction <1 year; most projects completed <3 years). Boiler modification schedule components and sequencing are described (permitting 12 months; commercial arrangements ~6 months; engineering/procurement ~7 months; site work ~3 months; construction ~4 months; startup/testing ~2 months), with pipeline availability preceding startup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital cost estimate for boiler modification
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA estimates average total capital cost to modify existing boilers to operate at up to 100% natural gas heat input is approximately $52 per kW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs vary by existing equipment and expected impacts on heat rate or steam temperature; Sargent & Lundy analysis informed the lower capital cost estimate relative to past EPA estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational (FOM) and fuel cost impacts of co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed O&M may not materially decrease because some coal-handling equipment may need continuous operation; incremental fuel costs reflect delivered price differentials between coal and gas and any net heat rate impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's 2030 reference case: delivered coal $1.56/MMBtu, natural gas $2.95/MMBtu, implying an incremental fuel cost of ~$1.39/MMBtu for substituting gas (assuming no heat rate change). EPA assumes a 1% average increase in net heat rate in cost estimates (affects total fuel cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost effectiveness and amortization assumptions for co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA estimates weighted average cost of 40% co-firing as the BSER is approximately $73 per ton CO2 reduced, or $13/MWh, assuming a 9-year amortization period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compared these estimates to cost reasonableness metrics (see separate entry). For sources with fundamentally different costs, states may consider those under RULOF provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness metrics used for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA compared co-firing costs against emission control cost benchmarks of $10.60 to $18.50 per MWh (EGU metric) and $98 per ton CO2e (2016 NSPS metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered fleet-average costs across various amortization periods (2 to 9 years) and found co-firing costs consistent with reasonableness metrics for the majority of sources that will operate past Jan 1, 2032.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA concluded co-firing is not expected to have significant adverse non-air quality health or environmental impacts; co-firing reduces coal-related pollutants (SO2, PM2.5, acid gases, mercury) proportionally to coal reduction and produces less NOx than coal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relied on existing pipeline safety and environmental regulations (PHMSA, FERC) to indicate pipeline transport can be safe with minimal environmental release risk; recent PHMSA and FERC rulemakings referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy requirements and efficiency impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-firing typically decreases boiler efficiency due to natural gas hydrogen content; for 20–100% co-firing, boiler efficiency expected to decrease 1–5%, but net unit heat rate effects vary and can be within approximately ±2%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because coal-handling auxiliary power demand usually decreases with co-firing, the overall net output efficiency may change slightly in either direction; site-specific analysis needed for exact net effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of CO2 emissions reductions from co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 emissions are reduced by approximately 4% for every additional 10% of co-firing. Moving from 100% coal to 60% coal/40% gas yields ~16% reduction in CO2 stack emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-CO2 pollutant co-benefits are similarly proportional to coal reduction; these reduction factors support EPA's selection of degree of emission limitation for medium-term units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation for technology advancement from co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because natural gas co-firing is already established and widely used, the rule is unlikely to spur significant technological advances or component cost reductions, though operational efficiencies may improve with greater use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of expected technological innovation does not preclude co-firing being BSER when other BSER criteria (demonstration, cost, impacts) are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of CCS as BSER for medium-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS is not finalized as the BSER for medium-term coal-fired units because the compliance/amortization window for those units (some retiring before Jan 1, 2039) would be less than ~7 years, making CCS capital costs exceed EPA's cost reasonableness metrics for the subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered the amortization period and cost reasonableness thresholds described elsewhere in the preamble and declined to select CCS for medium-term units on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Heat Rate Improvements (HRI) for medium-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat rate improvements were not considered BSER for medium-term steam generating units because achievable reductions are low and can produce a rebound effect whereby total emissions increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cited analysis in section VII.D.4.a for the rebound effect rationale; HRI may not produce net emissions benefits at the unit level for this subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of emission limitation determination and percent-based approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(d), after determining BSER EPA determines the degree of emission limitation achievable; due to large variation in emission rates among coal units, EPA finalizes degrees of limitation as percentage changes in emission rate (lb CO2/MWh-gross) over an extended period (e.g., annual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach yields standardized percent reductions that states can translate into standards of performance reflecting application of the BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific degrees of emission limitation finalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term coal-fired units (BSER = full-capture CCS at 90% capture): EPA finalizes an 88.4% reduction in emission rate (lb CO2/MWh-gross) over an extended period. Medium-term coal-fired units (BSER = 40% co-firing): EPA finalizes a 16% reduction in emission rate (lb CO2/MWh-gross) over an extended period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numerical percentages are the finalized degrees of emission limitation EPA used to define presumptive standards of performance and to inform state plan development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization of natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units by load level
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes subcategories for natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units based on annual capacity factor (load level): 'low', 'intermediate', and 'base' load groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcategorization is based on performance differences tied to annual capacity factor and is used to tailor BSER and presumptive standards for the different operational profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric definitions of load-level subcategories (gas/oil units)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes the load-level cutoffs as: low load = annual capacity factor < 8%; intermediate load = annual capacity factor >= 8% and < 45%; base load = annual capacity factor >= 45%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds were proposed and finalized to reflect observed performance distributions and to support appropriate selection of BSER and presumptive standards by load group.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER selection for natural gas- and oil-fired steam units: routine O&M
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes 'routine methods of operation and maintenance' as BSER for intermediate- and base-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: adequately demonstrated (units already employ these practices), negligible additional costs (no new technology or operational changes required), no adverse non-air quality/energy impacts, and such BSER prevents increases in emission rates even if it does not achieve unit-level CO2 reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER selection for low-load gas/oil units: uniform fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes a BSER of 'uniform fuels' for low-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units, with presumptive standards based on heat-input fuel composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: high variability in emission rates at low load makes lb CO2/MWh standards impractical; a heat-input based fuel composition standard (similar to prior NSPS 'clean fuels') is reasonable for low-load units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of alternative controls for gas/oil units (co-firing, CCS, hydrogen, HRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined co-firing is not applicable (these units already burn high shares of natural gas), CCS is not cost-effective due to low utilization (high capital cost and low 45Q tax credit potential), hydrogen co-firing is limited by availability and should be prioritized elsewhere, and HRI risks rebound effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered these alternatives and documented why routine O&M or uniform fuels are more appropriate BSER choices for the respective subcategories.
